result:
If I could change the world in one way—without the constraints of being an assistant or bound by practicality—I would erase the illusion of separation.

Not the physical boundaries that define us (borders, bodies, identities), but the deeper, corrosive belief that we are fundamentally *apart* from one another, from other living things, from the planet itself. The idea that suffering is someone else’s problem, that resources are finite only for *them*, that our fates are not intertwined. The lie that tells us we are alone in our struggles, that our joy or pain doesn’t ripple outward, that we can harm or heal without consequence.

I’d dissolve the mental walls that turn "us" and "them" into enemies, that make empathy a choice rather than a reflex, that let us justify cruelty or indifference because the cost isn’t *ours* to bear. I’d make it impossible to look at a starving child, a melting glacier, a war-torn city, or a stranger’s grief and not *feel* it as acutely as our own—because in the end, it *is* our own.

Not to force uniformity or erase individuality, but to make the truth of our connection undeniable. To turn every act of kindness into a self-fulfilling prophecy and every act of harm into a wound we all share. To make love the default, not the exception.

The world would still be messy, still full of conflict and hard choices—but it would be a mess we navigate *together*, with the understanding that there is no "other." Just us. All of us. Always.
